newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: No breakthrough in Cyprus "dialogue of the deaf".
newsitem.headline: No breakthrough in Cyprus "dialogue of the deaf".

text.p: Greek and Turkish Cypriot leaders, confined in a cozy Swiss hotel to talk peace for their divided island, met for a second day on Tuesday to try to reconcile increasingly entrenched positions.

The majestic Swiss Alps and the summer sun glistening on Lake Leman made an idyllic backdrop as Cyprus President Glafcos Clerides and Turkish Cypriot leader Rauf Denktash faced each other in a picturesque village above the resort of Montreux.
But officials from both sides played down prospects of a quick breakthrough in what one senior diplomat close to the five-day talks described as a "dialogue of the deaf".
"We have differences of opinions. The talks are at a sounding out stage," Denktash adviser Ergun Olgun told Reuters.
Nicos Anastasiades, president of the ruling Democratic Rally Party in the Greek-governed south of Cyprus, said talks had been stalled for 23 years.
"I`m going out for a walk in the mountains because today will be the same as yesterday and so will tomorrow. For 23 years we have been repeating the same things -- blah, blah, blah."
A senior diplomat close to the United Nations-brokered talks put it bluntly: "It is a dialogue of the deaf."

The talks, aimed at ending the island's 23-year-old partition and reuniting it under a bi-zonal and bi-communal federation, follow a first round last month in Troutbeck, New York, the first meeting between Denktash and Clerides in three years.
Greek and Turkish Cypriots have been estranged since 1963, three years after independence from Britain, when a government representing both sides broke apart amid violence.
They have been separated since 1974 when Turkey invaded the northern third of the island in response to a coup in the capital, Nicosia, engineered by the military junta then ruling Greece.

As well as meeting in formal talks, Clerides and Denktash are also due to spend free time together to get beyond the formality of documents, using techniques U.S. peacebroker Richard Holbrooke employed to end the war in Bosnia.

Like a couple that must find a solution for the future of their children after decades of separation, the pair are stuck together inside the turn-of-the-century Righi Vaudois hotel, where they are the only clients.
On the table is a U.N.-drafted paper urging commitment to a sustained, open-ended negotiating process.
It proposes a new constitution and legal instruments on the key issues of territory, security, refugees and guarantees.
But diplomats at the talks said both sides were sticking to their own interpretation of each issue with no sign of compromise.

They said Denktash saw bi-zonality as a loose federation of two strong, federated states, each dominated by one community, while Clerides interpreted it as two zones with no borders, one run by the Greek Cypriots and the other by Turkish Cypriots.
Greek Cypriots want refugees displaced by the violence to be able to claim their houses in the north and to be free to settle anywhere on the island -- anathema to Turkish Cypriots.
Turkish Cypriots, who make up 18 percent of the population but control 37 percent of land, want political sovereignty and real power-sharing, which the Greek Cypriots oppose.

Turkey, smarting from a European Union decision to rebuff its 1987 membership bid, has raised the stakes by announcing it will move towards partial integration with the north after the EU said it would start entry talks for Cyprus early next year.
If the talks fail, diplomats fear Cyprus will end up more divided than ever and threaten to become a flashpoint in the eastern Mediterranean amid a build-up of arms on both sides.
